claim: Microridges on zebrafish skin cells contain both actin and keratin filaments.
source: We found that microridges on zebrafish skin cells contained both actin and keratin filaments.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing colocalization of Krt17-GFP and Lifeact-mRuby in microridges (Figure 1C-E).

claim: Keratin filaments stabilize microridges.
source: Keratin filaments stabilized microridges, and overexpressing keratins lengthened them.
evidence: Supported by CK666 treatment experiments showing keratin patterns persist when F-actin is disrupted (Figure 2A-C), and time-lapse data showing microridges are more stable at later stages when keratins are present (Figure 8A-B).

claim: Overexpressing keratins lengthens microridges.
source: Keratin filaments stabilized microridges, and overexpressing keratins lengthened them.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing average microridge length per cell was longer in Krt17-GFP overexpressing cells than in wild-type cells (Figure 1F).

claim: Envoplakin and periplakin localize to microridges.
source: Envoplakin and periplakin, plakin family cytolinkers that bind F-actin and keratins, localized to microridges, and were required for their morphogenesis.
evidence: Supported by imaging of BAC reporters and endogenously tagged proteins showing Evpl and Ppl localization to microridges (Figure 3A-E).

claim: Envoplakin and periplakin are required for microridge morphogenesis.
source: Envoplakin and periplakin, plakin family cytolinkers that bind F-actin and keratins, localized to microridges, and were required for their morphogenesis.
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis showing ppl mutants lack microridges and evpl mutants form only short microridges (Figure 4A-B).

claim: Plakin protein levels directly dictate microridge length.
source: Strikingly, plakin protein levels directly dictate microridge length.
evidence: Supported by data showing heterozygous mutants have intermediate microridge lengths (Figure 4B), and overexpression of plakins lengthens microridges in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4D, Figure 6B, D).

claim: An actin-binding domain of periplakin is required to initiate microridge morphogenesis.
source: An actin-binding domain of periplakin was required to initiate microridge morphogenesis, whereas periplakin-keratin binding was required to elongate microridges.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing plakin head-rod fusions (lacking keratin-binding tail) can initiate microridge formation but not full elongation (Figure 6A-D).

claim: Periplakin-keratin binding is required to elongate microridges.
source: An actin-binding domain of periplakin was required to initiate microridge morphogenesis, whereas periplakin-keratin binding was required to elongate microridges.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing plakin constructs lacking keratin-binding domains or with mutations in keratin-binding sites cannot fully rescue microridge length (Figure 6A-D, Figure 7C-D).

claim: Intermediate filaments are not commonly believed to directly participate in the formation of cellular protrusions.
source: By contrast, IFs are not commonly believed to directly participate in the formation of cellular protrusions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of scientific knowledge/consensus in the field.

claim: Actin filaments create a wide variety of protrusions including filopodia, lamellipodia, invadopodia, and microvilli.
source: Actin filaments create a wide variety of well-studied protrusions, including filopodia, lamellipodia, invadopodia, and microvilli (Blanchoin et al., 2014; Pollard and Cooper, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Microtubules form cilia and flagella.
source: Similarly, microtubules form cilia and flagella (Mirvis et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Intermediate filaments are the strongest of the cytoskeletal elements.
source: The viscoelastic properties of IFs make them the strongest of the cytoskeletal elements.
evidence: Supported by citation to Janmey et al., 1991 study on mechanical properties of cytoskeletal filaments.

claim: Intermediate filaments rigidify and resist breakage at high strains, whereas actin filaments and microtubules break.
source: IFs deform at low strains, but, whereas actin filaments and microtubules break at high strains, IFs rigidify and resist breakage (Janmey et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janmey et al., 1991.

claim: Tetrameric IF subunits incorporate not only at filament ends, but also within filaments through intercalary exchange.
source: Tetrameric IF subunits incorporate not only at filament ends, but also within filaments, a process called 'intercalary exchange' that allows IFs to replace subunits without altering filament structure (Colakoğlu and Brown, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colakoğlu and Brown, 2009.

claim: Keratins are the most abundant IFs in epithelial cells.
source: Keratins are the most abundant IFs in epithelial cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about keratin distribution.

claim: Keratins organize and reinforce epithelial tissues by anchoring cells to one another and to the extracellular matrix at desmosomes and hemi-desmosomes.
source: They organize and reinforce epithelial tissues by anchoring cells to one another and to the extracellular matrix at desmosomes and hemi-desmosomes (Osmani and Labouesse, 2015), and they are bundled and cross-linked during the process of keratinization to create the cornified outer layers of mammalian skin (Eckhart et al., 2013; Smack et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Keratins support microvilli as part of the terminal web at their base.
source: Although keratins are not known to be directly involved in the morphogenesis of protrusions, they support microvilli as part of the terminal web at their base, where they interact with F-actin rootlets extending from microvilli, as well as myosin and other actin-binding proteins (Hirokawa et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirokawa et al., 1982.

claim: Keratins and vimentin have been detected in long invadopodia.
source: Keratins, along with the IF vimentin, have also been detected in long invadopodia (Schoumacher et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoumacher et al., 2010.

claim: Disrupting vimentin prevents full lengthening of invadopodia.
source: Although keratins themselves are not required for invadopodia morphogenesis, disrupting vimentin prevents their full lengthening, suggesting that IFs may play a role in the late stages of invadopodia extension (Schoumacher et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoumacher et al., 2010.

claim: Periplakin and envoplakin dimerize with each other and form hetero-oligomeric complexes.
source: The plakin family members periplakin (Ppl) and envoplakin (Evpl), which dimerize with each other and form hetero-oligomeric complexes (Kalinin et al., 2004), localize to desmosomes (DiColandrea et al., 2000) and are components of the cornified envelope in mammalian skin (Ruhrberg et al., 1997; Ruhrberg et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kalinin et al., 2004.

claim: Periplakin and envoplakin localize to desmosomes.
source: The plakin family members periplakin (Ppl) and envoplakin (Evpl), which dimerize with each other and form hetero-oligomeric complexes (Kalinin et al., 2004), localize to desmosomes (DiColandrea et al., 2000) and are components of the cornified envelope in mammalian skin (Ruhrberg et al., 1997; Ruhrberg et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to DiColandrea et al., 2000.

claim: Periplakin and envoplakin are components of the cornified envelope in mammalian skin.
source: The plakin family members periplakin (Ppl) and envoplakin (Evpl), which dimerize with each other and form hetero-oligomeric complexes (Kalinin et al., 2004), localize to desmosomes (DiColandrea et al., 2000) and are components of the cornified envelope in mammalian skin (Ruhrberg et al., 1997; Ruhrberg et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ruhrberg et al., 1997 and 1996.

claim: ppl and evpl knockout mice are viable.
source: ppl and evpl knockout mice are viable (Aho et al., 2004; Määttä et al., 2001), though skin barrier formation is delayed in evpl mutants (Määttä et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aho et al., 2004 and Määttä et al., 2001.

claim: Skin barrier formation is delayed in evpl mutant mice.
source: ppl and evpl knockout mice are viable (Aho et al., 2004; Määttä et al., 2001), though skin barrier formation is delayed in evpl mutants (Määttä et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Määttä et al., 2001.

claim: Evpl and Ppl have large N-terminal regions with direct actin-binding activity.
source: Evpl and Ppl have large N-terminal regions with direct actin-binding activity (Kalinin et al., 2005), as well as domains that associate with actin-binding proteins in other plakin family members (Jefferson et al., 2004; Sonnenberg and Liem, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kalinin et al., 2005.

claim: Plakins have rod domains that form coiled-coils mediating dimerization.
source: Plakins also have rod domains that form coiled-coils mediating dimerization (Kalinin et al., 2004), and C-terminal domains that bind to IFs (Karashima and Watt, 2002; Kazerounian et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kalinin et al., 2004.

claim: Plakins have C-terminal domains that bind to intermediate filaments.
source: Plakins also have rod domains that form coiled-coils mediating dimerization (Kalinin et al., 2004), and C-terminal domains that bind to IFs (Karashima and Watt, 2002; Kazerounian et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karashima and Watt, 2002 and Kazerounian et al., 2002.

claim: Microridges are laterally elongated protrusions arranged in maze-like patterns on the apical surface of epithelial cells.
source: In this study, we investigated the relationship between keratins, F-actin, and plakins in the morphogenesis of microridges, which are laterally elongated protrusions arranged in maze-like patterns on the apical surface of epithelial cells (Depasquale, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Depasquale, 2018.

claim: Microridges are required to maintain glycans on the skin surface.
source: Microridges are formed on a variety of mucosal epithelial cells, including cells that make up the outer layer of the zebrafish epidermis, called the periderm, where they are required to maintain glycans on the skin surface (Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pinto et al., 2019.

claim: Microridges are formed from the coalescence of finger-like, actin-based precursor protrusions called pegs.
source: Microridges are formed from the coalescence of finger-like, actin-based precursor protrusions called pegs (van Loon et al., 2020), a process dependent on the F-actin nucleator Arp2/3 (Lam et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2019; van Loon et al., 2020) and the relaxation of surface tension by cortical myosin-based contraction (van Loon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Loon et al., 2020.

claim: Microridge formation is dependent on the F-actin nucleator Arp2/3.
source: Microridges are formed from the coalescence of finger-like, actin-based precursor protrusions called pegs (van Loon et al., 2020), a process dependent on the F-actin nucleator Arp2/3 (Lam et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2019; van Loon et al., 2020) and the relaxation of surface tension by cortical myosin-based contraction (van Loon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lam et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2019; van Loon et al., 2020.

claim: Microridge formation depends on the relaxation of surface tension by cortical myosin-based contraction.
source: Microridges are formed from the coalescence of finger-like, actin-based precursor protrusions called pegs (van Loon et al., 2020), a process dependent on the F-actin nucleator Arp2/3 (Lam et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2019; van Loon et al., 2020) and the relaxation of surface tension by cortical myosin-based contraction (van Loon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Loon et al., 2020.

claim: Ultrastructural studies have reported the occasional presence of IFs within microridges.
source: Although studies of microridge morphogenesis have exclusively focused on F-actin regulation, like microvilli, microridges have keratins at their base, and ultrastructural studies have reported the occasional presence of IFs within microridges (Pinto et al., 2019; Schliwa, 1975; Uehara et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pinto et al., 2019; Schliwa, 1975; Uehara et al., 1991.

claim: Six type I keratin proteins are expressed in zebrafish periderm cells.
source: To investigate keratin localization in the zebrafish periderm, we tagged six type I keratin proteins expressed in periderm cells (Cokus et al., 2019) with GFP or mRuby at their C-termini, using bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cokus et al., 2019 and experimental data showing expression of six different keratin reporters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1).

claim: All six tagged keratins localized in two distinct patterns: a filamentous network filling cells and thick bundles in the pattern of microridges at the apical surface.
source: Imaging periderm cells in live zebrafish expressing these reporters revealed that all keratins localized in two distinct patterns within a cell: As expected, they formed a filamentous network filling cells; remarkably, they also formed what appeared to be thick bundles in the pattern of microridges at the apical surface (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data from six different keratin-GFP/mRuby BAC reporters.

claim: Endogenously tagged Krt17 localizes in both filamentous and microridge patterns.
source: Tagging an allele of one of these keratins, keratin 17 (Krt17), with CRISPR-facilitated homologous recombination, confirmed that the endogenously expressed protein localized in these two patterns (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging of endogenously tagged Krt17 using CRISPR knock-in.

claim: At 19 hpf, Krt17 forms a filamentous pattern in cells but does not localize within pegs.
source: At an early stage of microridge morphogenesis (19 hr post-fertilization, hpf), when periderm surfaces are dominated by pegs (van Loon et al., 2020), Krt17 formed the filamentous pattern in cells but did not localize within pegs.
evidence: Supported by SIM imaging data at 19 hpf (Figure 1C).

claim: At 48 hpf, Krt17 invades microridges where it appears to form filaments alongside F-actin.
source: At a later stage (48hpf), when mature microridges have formed, Krt17 invaded microridges, where it appeared to form filaments alongside F-actin (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by SIM imaging data at 48 hpf showing colocalization of Krt17 and F-actin (Figure 1C).

claim: Keratin localization to microridges increases as they lengthen.
source: Scoring the presence of keratin in protrusions of different lengths confirmed that the smallest protrusions, pegs, are largely devoid of keratin, and that keratin localization to microridges increased as they lengthened (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of keratin presence in protrusions of different sizes (Figure 1D-E).

claim: The apical Krt17-GFP microridge pattern is retained after 30 minutes of CK666 treatment despite loss of the F-actin microridge pattern.
source: Strikingly, despite the loss of the F-actin microridge pattern, the apical Krt17-GFP microridge pattern was retained (Figure 2A; Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification of overlap coefficients after CK666 treatment (Figure 2A, E).

claim: Overexpressing Krt17-GFP preserves protrusive membrane topology upon F-actin disruption.
source: Labeling cells with a membrane reporter (GFP-PH-PLC) revealed that overexpressing the Krt17-GFP BAC reporter preserved the protrusive membrane topology upon F-actin disruption (Figure 2B; Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing membrane protrusions persist in Krt17-overexpressing cells after CK666 treatment (Figure 2B-C).

claim: Evpl and Ppl are highly expressed and enriched in periderm cells relative to other epithelial cells.
source: By examining larval periderm cell transcriptomes (Cokus et al., 2019), we identified two potential cytolinker proteins, Evpl and Ppl, which are highly expressed and enriched in periderm cells, relative to other epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis cited from Cokus et al., 2019.

claim: Evpl and Ppl BAC reporters are expressed in periderm cells throughout the animal and are apparently exclusive to periderm cells.
source: These reporters were expressed in periderm cells throughout the animal and, as expected from genomic analyses (Cokus et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020), were apparently exclusive to periderm cells.
evidence: Supported by imaging of BAC reporters and citations to genomic analyses.

claim: When expressed on its own, Evpl forms prominent aggregates, which are reduced when Ppl is co-expressed.
source: Similar to its behavior in mammalian cell culture (DiColandrea et al., 2000), when expressed on its own, Evpl formed prominent aggregates, which were reduced when Ppl was co-expressed (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the possibility that the two plakin proteins dimerize or oligomerize.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing aggregates in Evpl-only expressing cells and reduction with Ppl co-expression (Figure 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Endogenously GFP-tagged Ppl localizes to microridges.
source: GFP-tagging the endogenous gene with CRISPR-facilitated homologous recombination verified the Ppl localization pattern (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by imaging of endogenously tagged Ppl (Figure 3C).

claim: Evpl and Ppl are localized within microridges adjacent to F-actin and keratin filaments but almost completely overlapping with each other in z-axis sections.
source: SIM microscopy of the co-expressed BAC reporters revealed that Evpl and Ppl were localized within microridges. In optical sections along the z-axis, Ppl and Evpl appeared to be adjacent to F-actin and keratin filaments but were almost completely overlapping with each other (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by SIM imaging data showing spatial relationships between Evpl, Ppl, F-actin, and keratins (Figure 3D).

claim: In x-y sections, Evpl and Ppl form an apparently alternating pattern.
source: In an x-y section, however, Evpl and Ppl formed an apparently alternating pattern, consistent with their ability to assemble into a higher order oligomeric arrangement (Kalinin et al., 2004; Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by Airyscan imaging showing alternating pattern (Figure 3E) and citation to Kalinin et al., 2004.

claim: At 19 hpf, Ppl associates with pegs and often forms longer and more continuous structures than F-actin.
source: Unlike Krt17, at this stage, Ppl associated with pegs and, surprisingly, often appeared to form longer and more continuous structures than F-actin itself (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data at 19 hpf (Figure 3F).

claim: Ppl forms elongated, continuous structures immediately before the coalescence of F-actin pegs into microridges.
source: These movies revealed that Ppl formed elongated, continuous structures immediately before the coalescence of F-actin pegs into microridges, potentially as part of a template for microridge assembly (Figure 3G, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging of cells undergoing cytokinesis (Figure 3G, Video 2).

claim: ppl mutants lack microridges, forming only pegs.
source: At larval stages, ppl mutants lacked microridges, forming only pegs, whereas evpl mutants formed pegs and short microridges (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification of microridge length in mutants (Figure 4A-B).

claim: evpl mutants form pegs and short microridges.
source: At larval stages, ppl mutants lacked microridges, forming only pegs, whereas evpl mutants formed pegs and short microridges (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification of microridge length in mutants (Figure 4A-B).

claim: Periderm cells in evpl−/−;ppl−/− double mutants are indistinguishable from those in ppl mutants, projecting only pegs.
source: Periderm cells in double mutants were indistinguishable from those in ppl mutants, projecting only pegs.
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification showing no significant difference between ppl single and double mutants (Figure 4A-B).

claim: Evpl and Ppl BAC reporters rescue microridge formation in each mutant.
source: Evpl and Ppl BAC reporters rescued microridge formation in each mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), demonstrating that the BAC fusions were functional and verifying that the mutations reduced gene function.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing microridge restoration in mutants expressing BAC reporters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: Morpholino antisense oligonucleotides targeting evpl and ppl cause similar microridge defects, which are rescued by expressing cDNAs of each gene.
source: This conclusion was further supported by the observation that morpholino antisense oligonucleotides targeting evpl and ppl caused similar microridge defects, which were rescued by expressing cDNAs of each gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown and cDNA rescue experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claim: Microridge defects persist through adulthood in both evpl and ppl genetic mutants.
source: Microridge defects persisted through adulthood in both genetic mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) but all single and double mutant animals were homozygous viable, fertile, and appeared morphologically normal at all stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining of adult scales (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).

claim: All single and double evpl/ppl mutant animals are homozygous viable, fertile, and appear morphologically normal at all stages.
source: Microridge defects persisted through adulthood in both genetic mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) but all single and double mutant animals were homozygous viable, fertile, and appeared morphologically normal at all stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by observation of mutant animals at larval and adult stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).

claim: Apical cell areas are comparable between wildtype and evpl/ppl single mutant larvae.
source: Apical cell areas were comparable between the wildtype and mutant larvae, indicating that these mutations do not cause cells to become dysmorphic or compromise apical constriction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification of apical cell areas (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Apical cell areas are significantly smaller in evpl−/−;ppl−/− double mutants compared to wildtype.
source: However, apical cell areas were, on average, significantly smaller in double mutants, suggesting that Evl and Ppl may play an unrelated, redundant role in restraining apical constriction.
evidence: Supported by quantification of apical cell areas showing significant difference in double mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).

claim: In evpl and ppl heterozygotes, average microridge length per cell is shorter than in WT cells but longer than in homozygous mutants.
source: Unexpectedly, in both evpl and ppl heterozygotes, average microridge length per cell was shorter than in WT cells but longer than in homozygous mutants (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification of microridge length in heterozygous mutants (Figure 4B).

claim: Average microridge length is shorter in trans-heterozygous mutants (evpl+/−; ppl+/−) than in either heterozygous mutant alone but longer than in homozygous mutants.
source: Average microridge length was shorter in trans-heterozygous mutants (evpl+/−; ppl+/−) than in either heterozygous mutant alone but longer than in homozygous mutants.
evidence: Supported by quantification of microridge length in trans-heterozygous mutants (Figure 4B).

claim: evpl and ppl mutants are semi-dominant.
source: These observations reveal that evpl and ppl mutants are semi-dominant and that the dose of plakin proteins dictates microridge length.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that heterozygotes have intermediate phenotypes.

claim: Cells expressing higher levels of plakins tend to have longer microridges.
source: Plotting fluorescence intensity versus average microridge length per cell revealed that cells expressing higher levels of plakins tended to have longer microridges (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of fluorescence intensity and microridge length (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).

claim: Microridges in cells with high plakin levels are substantially longer than microridges in WT cells.
source: Indeed, grouping cells into high- and low-expressing categories demonstrated that microridges in cells with high plakin levels were substantially longer than microridges in WT cells (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: Supported by quantification comparing high-expressing cells to WT (Figure 4D).

claim: The isolated head and tail domains of each plakin localize throughout the cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: As expected, full-length plakins localized to microridges, but the isolated head and tail domains of each plakin localized throughout the cytoplasm and nucleus, suggesting that dimerization via the rod domain is required for their localization to microridges (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by imaging of truncated plakin constructs (Figure 5A).

claim: Dimerization via the rod domain is required for plakin localization to microridges.
source: As expected, full-length plakins localized to microridges, but the isolated head and tail domains of each plakin localized throughout the cytoplasm and nucleus, suggesting that dimerization via the rod domain is required for their localization to microridges (Figure 5A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that isolated domains lacking the rod domain do not localize to microridges.

claim: The Ppl rod domain localizes variably to microridges.
source: The Ppl rod domain, which is required for dimerization in vitro (Kalinin et al., 2004), localized variably to microridges.
evidence: Supported by imaging of Ppl rod domain construct (Figure 5A) and citation to Kalinin et al., 2004.

claim: The Evpl rod domain does not localize to microridges.
source: However, the Evpl rod domain did not localize to microridges (Figure 5A), suggesting that it is not sufficient for dimerization, and implying that the Ppl rod domain may weakly homodimerize, as previously suggested by biochemical studies (Kalinin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by imaging of Evpl rod domain construct (Figure 5A) and citation to Kalinin et al., 2004.

claim: Full-length Ppl localizes to the short microridges in evpl mutants.
source: Indeed, whereas full-length Ppl localized to the short microridges in evpl mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), full-length Evpl was cytoplasmic in ppl mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the hypothesis that Ppl, but not Evpl, can homodimerize (or homo-oligomerize), and that dimerization is required for microridge localization.
evidence: Supported by imaging of full-length Ppl in evpl mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Full-length Evpl is cytoplasmic in ppl mutants.
source: Indeed, whereas full-length Ppl localized to the short microridges in evpl mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), full-length Evpl was cytoplasmic in ppl mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the hypothesis that Ppl, but not Evpl, can homodimerize (or homo-oligomerize), and that dimerization is required for microridge localization.
evidence: Supported by imaging of full-length Evpl in ppl mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Ppl, but not Evpl, can homodimerize or homo-oligomerize.
source: Indeed, whereas full-length Ppl localized to the short microridges in evpl mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), full-length Evpl was cytoplasmic in ppl mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the hypothesis that Ppl, but not Evpl, can homodimerize (or homo-oligomerize), and that dimerization is required for microridge localization.
evidence: Inferred from the differential localization of Ppl and Evpl in single mutants.

claim: ppl mutants have a more severe microridge phenotype than evpl mutants because Ppl can homodimerize but Evpl cannot.
source: This observation may also explain why ppl mutants have a more severe microridge phenotype than evpl mutants (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ppl can homodimerize and localize to microridges in evpl mutants, but Evpl cannot in ppl mutants.

claim: Head-rod fusions of both plakins localize to microridges more robustly than rod domains alone.
source: Head-rod fusions of both plakins localized to microridges more robustly than rod domains alone (Figure 5A), suggesting that the dimerized head domain enhances localization to microridges, potentially through F-actin binding.
evidence: Supported by imaging of head-rod fusion constructs (Figure 5A).

claim: The dimerized head domain enhances plakin localization to microridges, potentially through F-actin binding.
source: Head-rod fusions of both plakins localized to microridges more robustly than rod domains alone (Figure 5A), suggesting that the dimerized head domain enhances localization to microridges, potentially through F-actin binding.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that head-rod fusions localize better than rod alone, combined with knowledge that head domains bind F-actin.

claim: Ppl rod-tail domain fusions variably localize in keratin filament-like patterns.
source: Ppl, but not Evpl, rod-tail domain fusions variably localized in keratin filament-like patterns (Figure 5A), suggesting that the dimerized Ppl tail domain associates with keratins.
evidence: Supported by imaging of Ppl rod-tail fusion constructs (Figure 5A).

claim: The dimerized Ppl tail domain associates with keratins.
source: Ppl, but not Evpl, rod-tail domain fusions variably localized in keratin filament-like patterns (Figure 5A), suggesting that the dimerized Ppl tail domain associates with keratins.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ppl rod-tail fusions localize in keratin-like patterns.

claim: Shorter Ppl rod-tail fusions (sRT1-GFP and sRT2-GFP) are strongly localized in keratin-like patterns including microridge-associated bundles and the filamentous network throughout the cell.
source: Since parts of the rod domain can contribute to F-actin binding (Kalinin et al., 2005), we made two shorter fusions containing only part of the Ppl rod domain and the entire Ppl tail domain (sRT1-GFP and sRT2-GFP). These shorter fusions were strongly localized in keratin-like patterns that included the thick microridge-associated bundles and the filamentous network throughout the cell (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging of sRT1 and sRT2 constructs (Figure 5B-C).

claim: Dimerized plakins have the potential to link F-actin with keratins in microridges.
source: Together these findings demonstrate that dimerized plakins have the potential to link F-actin with keratins in microridges.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that head domains bind F-actin and tail domains bind keratins, and that dimerization is required for localization.

claim: Injecting genes encoding fluorescently tagged full-length Evpl-tdTomato and Ppl-GFP into evpl−/−;ppl−/− double mutant fish rescues microridge development.
source: Injecting genes encoding fluorescently tagged full-length Evpl-tdTomato and Ppl-GFP into evpl−/−;ppl−/− double mutant fish rescued microridge development (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing microridge restoration (Figure 6A).

claim: Average microridge length per cell correlates with plakin fluorescence intensity in rescue experiments.
source: Strikingly, the average microridge length per cell correlated with fluorescence intensity (Figure 6B), further illustrating that plakin expression levels determine microridge length.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis in rescue experiments (Figure 6B).

claim: Truncated fusion proteins lacking the plakin head domains do not rescue microridge length in double mutants.
source: By contrast, truncated fusion proteins lacking the plakin head domains did not rescue microridge length in double mutants (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with rod-tail fusions (Figure 6A-B).

claim: Ppl rod-tail fusions do not rescue Ppl single mutants.
source: Similarly, Ppl rod-tail fusions did not rescue Ppl single mutants (Figure 6C–D), suggesting that heterodimers containing only the Evpl head domain cannot support microridge morphogenesis.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments in ppl mutants (Figure 6C-D).

claim: Heterodimers containing only the Evpl head domain cannot support microridge morphogenesis.
source: Similarly, Ppl rod-tail fusions did not rescue Ppl single mutants (Figure 6C–D), suggesting that heterodimers containing only the Evpl head domain cannot support microridge morphogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ppl rod-tail fusions (which would heterodimerize with endogenous Evpl) do not rescue ppl mutants.

claim: Evpl and Ppl head-rod domain fusions rescue the initiation of microridge formation but not microridge length in double mutants.
source: To ask if plakin-keratin interactions play a role in microridge morphogenesis, we expressed tagged Evpl and Ppl head-rod domain fusions, which lack the keratin-binding tail domain, in double mutant embryos. These fusions rescued the initiation of microridge formation but did not rescue microridge length as well as full-length plakins (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with head-rod fusions (Figure 6A-B).

claim: The Evpl and Ppl dimerized head domains are sufficient for the initiation of microridge morphogenesis but not for their full elongation.
source: These results indicate that the Evpl and Ppl dimerized head domains are sufficient for the initiation of microridge morphogenesis but not for their full elongation.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing head-rod fusions can initiate but not fully elongate microridges.

claim: Expressing the Ppl head-rod fusion in ppl single mutants allows the formation of only short, but not fully elongated, microridges.
source: Similarly, expressing the Ppl head-rod fusion in ppl single mutants allowed the formation of only short, but not fully elongated, microridges (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments in ppl mutants (Figure 6C-D).

claim: Plakin-keratin association facilitates microridge elongation.
source: Together these experiments suggest that plakin-keratin association facilitates microridge elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that constructs lacking keratin-binding domains cannot fully elongate microridges.

claim: The DWEEI amino acid sequence in the Ppl tail domain is required for keratin binding.
source: To further test if plakin-keratin interactions promote microridge elongation, we deleted five amino acids in the Ppl tail domain required for keratin binding (∆DWEEI) (Figure 7A; Karashima and Watt, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karashima and Watt, 2002.

claim: Localization of Ppl(∆DWEEI) rod-tail fusions to the keratin network is severely reduced.
source: Localization of Ppl(∆DWEEI) rod-tail fusions (sRT2[∆DWEEI]-GFP) to the keratin network was severely reduced (Figure 7B), confirming in vivo that this site is required for optimal Ppl-keratin binding.
evidence: Supported by imaging of Ppl(∆DWEEI) constructs (Figure 7B).

claim: Ppl(∆DWEEI) cannot rescue microridge length in ppl mutants as well as WT Ppl.
source: Similar to head-rod fusions, Ppl(∆DWEEI) could not rescue microridge length in ppl mutants as well as WT Ppl.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with Ppl(∆DWEEI) (Figure 7C-D).

claim: Deleting the 1/2Box2 domain in Ppl yields similar results to deleting DWEEI.
source: Deleting another small domain required for keratin binding (∆1/2Box2) (Karashima and Watt, 2002) in Ppl yielded similar results (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with Ppl(∆1/2Box2) (Figure 7C-D) and citation to Karashima and Watt, 2002.

claim: Ppl-keratin interactions are required for full microridge elongation.
source: These findings suggest that Ppl-keratin interactions are required for full microridge elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutations disrupting keratin binding prevent full microridge elongation.

claim: Short, nascent microridges at 24 hpf are less stable than longer keratin-containing microridges at 48 hpf.
source: Over the course of 5 minute time-lapse movies, the microridge pattern changed more rapidly at 24hpf than at 48hpf, indicating that shorter microridges likely lacking keratins are less stable than longer keratin-containing microridges in older animals (Figure 8A–B, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging and overlap coefficient analysis at different developmental stages (Figure 8A-B, Video 3).

claim: Microridges are more dynamic in cells expressing Evpl and Ppl head-rod fusions than those expressing full-length plakins at 48 hpf.
source: To test if plakin-keratin binding plays a role in stabilization, we compared cells in double mutant animals expressing full-length Evpl and Ppl to those expressing the Evpl and Ppl head-rod domains (i.e. ∆tail domain) at 48hpf. Microridges were more dynamic in cells expressing Evpl and Ppl head-rod fusions than those expressing full-length plakins (Figure 8C–D, Video 4), similar to microridges in WT cells of younger animals.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging and overlap coefficient analysis comparing full-length and head-rod fusions (Figure 8C-D, Video 4).

claim: Plakin-keratin interactions stabilize microridges to allow them to elongate.
source: These results suggest that plakin-keratin interactions stabilize microridges to allow them to elongate.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that microridges lacking keratin binding (via head-rod fusions) are more dynamic and shorter.

claim: Microridge morphogenesis proceeds through at least three molecularly separable steps: peg formation, peg coalescence to form nascent microridges, and microridge elongation.
source: Thus, microridge morphogenesis proceeds through at least three molecularly separable steps: (1) peg formation, (2) peg coalescence to form nascent microridges, and (3) microridge elongation (Figure 8E).
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing distinct molecular requirements at different stages.

claim: Evpl and Ppl are first required for the coalescence of pegs into microridges.
source: Evpl and Ppl are first required for the coalescence of pegs into microridges, since periderm cells in evpl and ppl mutants retain pegs, but microridges are reduced or absent in these mutants (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that plakin mutants have pegs but lack or have reduced microridges.

claim: The plakins may guide peg coalescence by forming oligomers.
source: This observation suggests the intriguing possibility that the plakins, which can form oligomers on their own in vitro (Kalinin et al., 2004), guide peg coalescence.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Ppl forms continuous structures before F-actin coalescence and the known ability of plakins to oligomerize.

claim: Peg coalescence requires the Arp2/3 actin branch nucleating complex.
source: Peg coalescence requires not only the plakin proteins, but also the Arp2/3 actin branch nucleating complex (Lam et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2019; van Loon et al., 2020) and actomyosin contraction (van Loon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Peg coalescence requires actomyosin contraction.
source: Peg coalescence requires not only the plakin proteins, but also the Arp2/3 actin branch nucleating complex (Lam et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2019; van Loon et al., 2020) and actomyosin contraction (van Loon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Loon et al., 2020.

claim: Evpl and Ppl likely contribute to peg coalescence by interacting directly with F-actin or actin regulators.
source: Thus, it is likely that Evpl and Ppl contribute to peg coalescence by interacting directly with F-actin or actin regulators, helping to incorporate the actin bundles within pegs into the larger actin network of microridges.
evidence: This is inference based on the known actin-binding properties of plakin head domains and their requirement for peg coalescence.

claim: Evpl and Ppl recruit keratins into microridges to instigate the elongation step of morphogenesis.
source: We thus propose that Evpl and Ppl recruit keratins into microridges to instigate the subsequent elongation step of morphogenesis (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined experimental results.

claim: Overexpressing Krt17 preserved the three-dimensional structure of microridges upon F-actin disruption.
source: Perhaps most compellingly, overexpressing Krt17 preserved the three-dimensional structure of microridges upon F-actin disruption (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing membrane protrusions persist in Krt17-overexpressing cells after CK666 treatment (Figure 2A-C).

claim: Keratins provide microridges with stability.
source: Together these observations indicate that keratins provide microridges with stability.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including keratin persistence after F-actin disruption and increased stability of keratin-containing microridges.

claim: Vimentin has been hypothesized to play a role in the growth of invadopodia at a late morphogenetic step.
source: Notably, the IF vimentin has also been hypothesized to play a role in the growth of invadopodia at a late morphogenetic step (Schoumacher et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoumacher et al., 2010.

claim: Vimentin may stabilize invadopodia to allow them to elongate, similar to keratin in microridges.
source: Perhaps vimentin, similar to keratin in microridges, stabilizes invadopodia to allow them to elongate.
evidence: This is speculation based on the parallel between keratin function in microridges and vimentin in invadopodia.

claim: Intermediate filaments can preserve their form even as subunits are replaced.
source: A role for IFs as microridge stabilizers is consistent with the fact that IFs are intrinsically stronger than the other cytoskeletal elements, and can preserve their form even as subunits are replaced (Colakoğlu and Brown, 2009; Janmey et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colakoğlu and Brown, 2009 and Janmey et al., 1991.

claim: The extreme stability of stereocilia reflects the fact that there is little F-actin turnover within them.
source: The extreme stability of stereocilia reflects the fact that there is little F-actin turnover within them (Narayanan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012), whereas microvilli maintain their morphologies despite constant actin turnover (Loomis et al., 2003; Meenderink et al., 2019; Tyska and Mooseker, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Narayanan et al., 2015 and Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: Microvilli maintain their morphologies despite constant actin turnover.
source: The extreme stability of stereocilia reflects the fact that there is little F-actin turnover within them (Narayanan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012), whereas microvilli maintain their morphologies despite constant actin turnover (Loomis et al., 2003; Meenderink et al., 2019; Tyska and Mooseker, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Loomis et al., 2003; Meenderink et al., 2019; Tyska and Mooseker, 2002.

claim: Microridges constantly replace their F-actin scaffolds.
source: Like microvilli, microridges constantly replace their F-actin scaffolds, since inhibiting Arp2/3 leads to disassembly of the microridge F-actin network within thirty minutes (Lam et al., 2015; van Loon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lam et al., 2015 and van Loon et al., 2020.

claim: Microridges require keratins to preserve their forms in the face of F-actin turnover.
source: However, in contrast to microvilli, microridges require keratins to preserve their forms in the face of F-actin turnover, perhaps because their more extended morphologies and less organized F-actin networks (Pinto et al., 2019) require additional stabilization.
evidence: This is inference based on the experimental results showing keratins stabilize microridges and citation to Pinto et al., 2019 about F-actin organization.

claim: By combining F-actin with IFs, microridges may achieve an optimal balance between plasticity and stability.
source: A landmark study comparing the three classes of cytoskeletal elements speculated that the mechanical 'differences between F-actin and vimentin are optimal for the formation of a composite material with a range of properties that cannot be achieved by a single polymer network' (Janmey et al., 1991). By combining F-actin with IFs, microridges may achieve an optimal balance between plasticity and stability.
evidence: This is speculation based on the citation to Janmey et al., 1991 and the experimental findings.
